_about: Hand-authored map of DATAGLOW's documented capabilities to the js/ code that backs them. Consumed by .github/scripts/capability-drift.mjs (npm run test:capdrift) to keep docs/capability-map.md and README claims honest against shipped code. When you add, remove, or repurpose a js/ module, update this manifest and the capability map in the SAME PR (see AGENTS.md). Each capability lists the file(s) that MUST exist for it to be real, and — for the identity-defining modules — a symbol that must still be exported.
_platforms: Each capability declares a non-empty `platforms` list — a subset of ["browser","desktop","mobile"] — read at runtime by js/app-shell/capability-registry.js to decide which capability modules to dynamically import on the detected runtime (plain browser vs. Tauri desktop shell; mobile is forward-looking and unused today). browser+desktop is the default: the Tauri v1 shell is 'a browser tab in a native window', so anything that works in the browser works there too. A capability is browser-only when it depends on a browser web API the desktop shell deliberately excludes (e.g. the File System Access API — see docs/desktop-shell.md); it is desktop-only when it needs a Tauri/Node native API a plain browser lacks (none today). When a single capability groups files with different reach, an optional `platformsByFile` map overrides `platforms` per file (the capability-level list stays the union of where the capability as a whole is usable).

Metric Contract Status (the contract answer the readiness gate always wanted)
capabilities.notes: computeReadinessGate() has always taken a metricContractStatus argument and refused to call a dataset agent-consumable when a contract was broken, but nothing in the running app ever produced that object, so the check was wired and permanently fed null. Five readers of state.metricContractStatus (the readiness badge, the trust certificate, the agent gate, the guarded copilot and the MCP gate exporter) had zero writers. This module is the producer, and js/app-shell/main.js now assigns it whenever a definition is saved. Broken means the definition the app is using right now no longer matches the latest version recorded in that metric's own history, which is drift away from the agreed contract. A metric with no recorded history is untracked, not violated, and a metric with many versions is not broken: change is the point. Honestly scoped: every human save path in Metric Studio records a version in the same breath, so in-app drift is not reachable through the UI today and the immediate value is turning 'contracts were not checked' into 'every contracted definition still matches'. It becomes a real alarm the first time any writer reaches MetricRegistry.update() without recording a version, which the tests pin rather than assume. It only reads, and it records nothing, because recording a version is a human-confirmed mutation.

capabilities.description: Organization-level policy engine for managed deployments. IT administrators drop a dataglow-policy.json alongside index.html to disable BYOK Story (external LLM), WebRTC Rooms, CDN fetches (air-gapped environments), and federated learning before any feature flag is evaluated. Active policy shows an ENTERPRISE badge in the nav and locks affected feature toggles. Default open -- no policy file means full consumer mode.

PHI Shield
capabilities.notes: One-button on-device PHI/Safe Harbor screen + AI prompt guard. Screening aid only.

capabilities.name: Notebook to App
capabilities.notes: Save as app on the Python and R notebook toolbars: turns a notebook that already ran on this device into ONE self-contained HTML file (cells, captured text output, captured plots) that opens by double click with no server, no install and no internet. A confirm sheet lists what goes in the file and nothing is written until the human presses Save. PHI Shield scans first and a hit preselects leaving results out; the builder refuses to emit a file that references anything off the device. Zero-upload.

capabilities.notes: Wide-to-long reshape with preview/apply; pure transform + DuckDB SQL glass-box.

capabilities.name: Repair Recipe Library
capabilities.notes: Save/list/reapply Excel Hell (and Guided Unpivot) prep recipes on-device via a standalone IndexedDB. Metadata only (steps + column names), never raw rows. Preview-first; Apply is click-only.

capabilities.name: Mobile PHI chip + first-run calm
capabilities.notes: Calm chrome pass over the existing PHI Shield: short never-truncated privacy labels, 44px safe-area-aware topbar chip, and a quiet first-run strip (on-device promise + one Load CTA, no auto-dismiss timer). Additive; does not change PHI detection.

capabilities.name: Shield Packs (domain privacy packs, PHI is pack 0)
capabilities.notes: One calm surface listing four on-device privacy packs. Pack 0 is the existing PHI Shield, reused via window.DataGlowPhiShield rather than reimplemented. Finance PII, Privilege labels, and Justice sensitive add shape/label detectors plus a combined posture; the Justice pack fails closed (blocks AI and export paths, shows a high-sensitivity banner). Session-scoped, in-memory, never uploads rows.

capabilities.name: Trust Ledger (session trust events, hash chained)
capabilities.notes: One append-only list of this session's trust events, oldest first, behind a Trust button next to Air-Gap and Shield Packs. Rows are plain sentences plus a hash prefix, chained with SHA-256 using the same genesis anchor and canonical-JSON discipline as js/provenance/provenance.js and the AI Touch Ledger, so it composes the existing provenance rather than adding a second crypto stack; a drift test pins the digest against provenance.js. Verify re-walks the chain and names an edit, reorder or deletion. Malformed input becomes a visibly refused row rather than a dropped one. Session-scoped and in memory: no localStorage, cookies, IndexedDB or network, and the text/Markdown/JSON buttons write one file to this device. Rows come from the events the app already fires (dataglow:pulse-scored, dataglow:export-triggered) plus explicit record() callers such as the Save-as-app sheet. A record of this session, not an audit certification.

capabilities.name: Publish-Safe (one gate before anything is written or shared)
capabilities.notes: Combines the four checks DataGlow already had but no export path asked together: PHI Shield on the exact text that would travel, the readiness gate on the dataset behind it, Metric Contracts on whether definitions are still the agreed ones, and Air-Gap Mode on whether the human asked for nothing to cross the network. Returns one plain-language verdict of clear, caution or blocked plus a suggested safer default. Sensitive values leaving the device is the one hard refusal, because a file that has left cannot be unshared; sensitive values staying on the device is a caution with results preselected out, since the human owns the disk. Failing readiness or a drifted metric definition is a caution, never a block, because those are quality signals and not privacy ones. A check that could not run is never reported as a pass, and a caller whose artifact has no dataset behind it must pass readiness 'not-applicable' out loud rather than getting that by silence. Wired into the Save-as-app confirm sheet today, where it shows the verdict and records the outcome in the Trust Ledger. Pure: gathers no evidence itself, mutates nothing, decides nothing for the human. There is no off-device export path in the tree today, so the refusal branch guards the Air-Gap egress case and any future destination rather than a path that ships now.

capabilities.name: Air-Gap Mode
capabilities.notes: One session-scoped switch that hard-blocks DataGlow's outbound paths (AI, MCP, server offload, CDN runtime downloads, telemetry, Rooms, federated learning) while local DuckDB/SQL/Python/R/charts keep running. Fails closed: anything not on the on-device allowlist is blocked while active. In-memory only, nothing written to storage. Complements the administrator-set Enterprise No-Egress policy; this is the user's own switch. Not a firewall.

capabilities.name: Explain (plain language over evidence that already exists)
capabilities.notes: Answers the question a person actually asks of a result, which is not what the numbers are but whether they can be relied on. Composes rather than computes: every sentence traces to one of seven sources that already ran and published, and the engine gathers no evidence of its own. Confidence is derived from how many of those sources answered, so a panel built on two checks out of seven cannot present itself as well-evidenced. A source that could not run is named as an unknown, never dropped and never reported as a pass, because the failure mode worth engineering against is a missing check reading as clean. All on-device: no network is touched, so it works identically with Air-Gap Mode on. The canvas panel reads the same gates GlassBox reads, which is what keeps the plain-language summary and the show-the-math block from contradicting each other. Pure engine, browser-only surface.

capabilities.name: GlassBox (show the math under a finding)
capabilities.notes: Finding on top, proof underneath, in the same shape on every surface that has one. The proof is the literal code that ran plus the engine that ran it, read from the paired editor at open time rather than reconstructed, because a reconstructed query looks checkable and can be wrong. Badges come only from gates that genuinely reported; an absent gate yields no chip and the panel states that an absence of evidence is not a clean result, which is the difference between this and a green tick that means nothing. Wired on the three real result surfaces today: the SQL view result, the SQL tab result and the Python result. Guided Unpivot is deliberately left alone because it already has its own glass-box toggle and two answers to one question is worse than one. Pure engine, browser-only surface.

capabilities.name: Compare to prior period (month, week or day over the one before)
capabilities.notes: Aggregates a metric into calendar periods, per entity when the table has one, and puts the prior period's value, the delta and the percent change beside each. Prior means the previous CALENDAR period, computed by stepping the calendar back one grain and looking that key up, NOT the previous row: LAG would compare March against January whenever February is missing and label it month over month, which is a wrong number that looks reasonable on a chart. A missing prior period yields null for the prior, null for the delta, and a plain note saying how many periods had no predecessor. Percent change is null rather than Infinity when the prior is zero, and the delta is still reported in that case. SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX and COUNT are offered because picking SUM for an average is the same class of silent error. The glass-box SQL is a self LEFT JOIN on the stepped-back period key so the proof matches the rows a person sees. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network, so it runs with Air-Gap Mode on.

capabilities.name: Join on date range (event date inside a span)
capabilities.notes: Matches each event to the reference rows whose span contains its date, with an optional key. The capability that earns the module is previewDateRangeJoin(), which counts matched rows, unmatched rows, the worst fanout and how many events fall inside more than one range WITHOUT materializing the join, so the fanout is knowable before a person confirms. Overlapping reference ranges are the hazard: one day of overlap silently duplicates every event on that day, and every total taken afterwards is quietly larger, with each individual row still looking correct. Two boundary rules are explicit and configurable rather than assumed, and both appear in the generated non-equi SQL: a blank end date means still in force (an explicit OR end IS NULL), and bounds are inclusive on both sides (a <= rather than a <). An end date that is present but unreadable is never read as open, since that would extend a closed range to forever. Preview and apply share one matching function so they cannot disagree.

capabilities.name: First or last event per entity
capabilities.notes: One row per group chosen by an order column, or every row kept with its rank. This exists for ties rather than for ordering: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY entity ORDER BY ts DESC) is free to return either of two rows sharing a timestamp and may return a different one on the next run or a different engine, which produces a report that changes when nothing changed. The tie-break here is total and stated: after the order column, rows are compared by every remaining column in table order. That makes the answer a function of the table's contents alone, identical in the JS engine and in the generated DuckDB QUALIFY / ROW_NUMBER SQL, where the full tie-break appears in the ORDER BY rather than only in a comment. When ties actually occurred the notes report how many and say plainly that the choice was repeatable but arbitrary, because determinism is not meaning. Rows with no readable order value are excluded and counted, never defaulted to the epoch where they would win the first slot.

capabilities.name: As-of lookup (the value that was in force on that date)
capabilities.notes: For each fact row, the reference row with the greatest effective date at or before the fact's date, with an optional key. It prevents the most expensive error in this bundle: joining a sale to a price table on product id alone returns today's price, and today's price multiplied by last year's units is revenue that never happened, in a number that looks completely ordinary and will be quoted in a meeting. Three refusals are deliberate and reported. A fact dated before every reference row gets NULL, never the oldest row on record, because the oldest value is not the value that was true then. Two reference rows sharing one effective date are a genuine ambiguity in the reference table, so the later one in table order is used and the count is named. A fact whose date cannot be read is blanked and counted rather than looked up as of today. Lookup columns always arrive with an _asof suffix so a point-in-time value cannot be mistaken for a current one. The glass-box SQL is DuckDB's ASOF LEFT JOIN with the equivalent ROW_NUMBER form underneath for engines that lack it.

capabilities.name: Expand a hierarchy into node, parent, depth and path
capabilities.notes: Turns a parent/child column pair or a single path column into one row per node carrying its depth, its parent, the root it sits under, its full path and whether it is a leaf. The decisions that matter are about broken trees, because real org charts and account hierarchies are broken. A node whose parent id is not in the table is a root for the purposes of the walk and is reported as one rather than silently dropped. A node that is its own ancestor is not followed forever: the walk carries its visited list, stops at 256 levels, and emits the nodes it could never reach with a null depth and an in_cycle marker, so a self-referencing row produces a finding instead of a hung tab. The glass-box SQL is a WITH RECURSIVE CTE seeded on the rows with no findable parent and carrying the same visited list, so the cycle guard a person reads is the guard the rows came from. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network, so it runs with Air-Gap Mode on.

capabilities.name: Nested lists into rows, with the row count shown first
capabilities.notes: Turns a column of JSON arrays or separated text into one row per element, repeating the other columns. Two things separate it from a split. The row count comes first: previewNestedToRows() counts the output WITHOUT building it, so the panel states "1,204 rows would become 38,911" and raises its warnings above the run button, while it is still free to change the settings. And an empty list is kept rather than dropped: a plain UNNEST removes those rows silently, and a row disappearing from a count is far harder to notice than a blank cell, so by default the row survives with a blank element and the count is reported. Dropping them is available and stated. A cell that looks like JSON and does not parse is reported as unreadable rather than split on a comma and passed off as a list. Complementary to the semi-structured JSON flattener in js/ingestion/json-flattener.js, which widens an object into columns; this lengthens a list into rows. Glass-box SQL is the DuckDB UNNEST form, written with the LEFT JOIN that keeps the empty rows. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network.

capabilities.name: Fill blanks and always flag the cells that were filled
capabilities.notes: Forward fill from the last value above, or a constant chosen by the person. Every filled column gets a companion _was_filled boolean column, and that is deliberately not configurable: an invented value that reads like a measured one is the entire risk here, and a fill with no flag is indistinguishable downstream from data that was always there. Only two modes ship. A group mean or median needs its own account of what it assumes, and js/cleaning/imputation.js already offers the statistical modes, so rather than duplicating them the runtime notes name that wizard and say plainly that it does not add a flag column, which is the difference a person choosing between the two needs to know. Forward fill requires an order column, and rows whose order value cannot be read sort last and are never filled, because carrying a value into a row whose position is unknown is guessing twice. The glass-box SQL is last_value(...) IGNORE NULLS over an unbounded preceding window, with the IGNORE NULLS called out as the load-bearing part. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network.

capabilities.name: A start and end date into one row per calendar day
capabilities.notes: Turns a start and end date per row into one row per calendar day, which is the occupancy, bed-days and licence-coverage shape. This is the largest multiplier in the transforms set, so the count comes before the rows: previewExpandDateRange() counts the days without building any, warns at 100,000 output rows and at 20,000 on a narrow screen, and refuses outright above 2,000,000 BEFORE anything is built, so a refusal never leaves the caller holding a half-expanded table. There is deliberately no option to run an open range up to today. An open-ended range is skipped unless the person states an as-at date, and that date is written into both the notes and the generated SQL as a literal, because a table built against current_date gives a different answer every time it is built and nobody can reproduce last month's number from it. An end date that is present but unreadable is not treated as open, since reading a mistyped date as "still going" would stretch a closed range to the as-at date. The end day counts by default and the notes state which convention was used, because both are in real use and which is right depends on whether the end date is the last day or the day it ended. Glass-box SQL is a CROSS JOIN LATERAL generate_series. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network.

capabilities.name: Group a number column into bands, with the histogram from the same counts
capabilities.notes: Equal-width bands by default, or edges typed by hand. The histogram is drawn from the same binCounts() the apply uses rather than from a separate pass over the rows, so the bars a person read and the bands they applied cannot come to disagree; that also makes the picture testable in Node without a canvas. Equal-width binning is quietly wrong on skewed columns, where one very large value stretches the range and everything else lands in the first band, so the engine warns when a single band holds 90 percent or more of the rows in range and points at custom edges. Bands are half-open, said in the labels, in the notes and in the generated CASE ladder, with only the top band including its own upper edge, so the largest value has somewhere to go. A value outside the edges gets a blank band rather than being pushed into the nearest one, because the values that fell outside are exactly the ones worth looking at, and the CASE ladder therefore ends in ELSE NULL rather than a catch-all band. A column with no spread is reported as such instead of being split into ten bands that would imply a range that is not there. Separate from the chart histogram in js/chart/chart-engine.js, which draws a picture; this adds a column. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network.

capabilities.name: Keep the most recent record per group, and name what was discarded
capabilities.notes: Entity keys plus an order column leave one row per group. Unlike the first/last event transform, which answers a question about events that were never wanted, this DELETES rows that were in the table a moment ago, and the whole risk is that they were not duplicates at all. So the number it leads with is not "rows removed" but "rows removed that disagreed": dropping an exact copy of a row loses nothing, while dropping a row that shared the key and held a different address, amount or diagnosis is throwing away a fact, and those two cases have the same row count. The result counts the conflicting groups separately and names the columns where the discarded rows disagreed with the row kept, which is what tells a person whether this was a de-duplication or a choice about the data. Ties on the order column are broken by every remaining column in table order, identically in the engine and in the generated ROW_NUMBER SQL, and the notes admit that repeatable is not the same as correct. A row whose order value cannot be read is kept by default and never wins a group that has a dated row, because deleting a row on the strength of a mistyped date is a loss nobody asked for. It shares sortableOrderValue, compareSortable and compareValues with the first/last event engine through js/transforms/transform-core.js rather than copying them, so the two cannot come to disagree about what latest means. Rows come out in the order their groups were first seen, so a diff against the original stays readable. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network.

capabilities.name: Consecutive runs of active days, counted in days rather than in rows
capabilities.notes: Gaps-and-islands over an entity plus a date column, giving one row per unbroken streak with its start, its end and its length. The thing this refuses to get wrong is that a streak is a run of DAYS and not a run of ROWS. Two rows carrying the same date are one active day, so a table where an export ran twice does not produce longer streaks than the same table imported once; the collapsed rows are counted and named in the notes rather than silently absorbed, because a large number there usually means the export and not the entity. The generated SQL leads with SELECT DISTINCT over the entity and the cast date for exactly that reason, and only then subtracts a ROW_NUMBER from the date to form the island key, so a reader can see which step is doing the work. A run that reaches the last day in the data has not ended, it has run out of data, and the difference matters when the number is quoted: an optional as-of date adds a still_running column and the notes say how many runs are open, while with no as-of date no claim about ending is made at all. Rows whose date cannot be read are dropped and counted, never quietly treated as a gap that would split one streak into two. A minimum length hides short runs but the hidden count is reported, so the visible rows are never mistaken for all of them. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network.

capabilities.name: Moving average with an honest warm-up, and crossovers that need two rows to exist
capabilities.notes: A trailing average over an ordered column, optionally a second window, optionally a column marking where the two cross. The silent wrongness this exists to stop is a seven row average of two rows presented as a seven row average: on a chart the two are indistinguishable, and the early points are the ones people read as a trend. So warm-up rows are blank by default, every row carries rows_in_window stating how many values actually went into it, and the partial mode is offered but says in the notes that those early rows are not comparable to the later ones. The crossover column requires both averages on the current row AND on the row before it, which is what stops the first row where both exist being reported as a crossing; that false signal at the start of a series is the most common way a crossover column gets read as a real event. A window counted in rows over a series with missing days covers more calendar than its label claims, so calendar gaps inside the window are detected and stated rather than left for the reader to notice. Grouping restarts the window per series, so no average silently mixes two entities at their boundary. Two identical windows are refused outright, because the crossover column they would produce is always empty and reads as no signal rather than as a configuration mistake. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network.

capabilities.name: Counts for a multi-value column, with both percentage denominators shown and labelled
capabilities.notes: A column holding several values in one cell is split and counted per category rather than per combination, so a cell reading Cardiology; Endocrinology stops being its own bucket of one and starts counting toward both categories. Splitting makes the counts sum to more than the number of records, which is what multi-membership means and is not an error. The error is presenting those counts against a denominator that implies they are exclusive: percentages that sum to 180 get quietly rescaled by a reader into something that adds to 100, and the conclusion drawn from it is wrong. So every count carries TWO labelled percentages. pct_of_records is the share of records carrying the value and sums above 100 whenever any record holds several; pct_of_mentions is the share of all values mentioned and sums to 100. Both are shown because either one alone gets misread as the other, and the notes state the actual sum out loud whenever it exceeds 100. A record is counted once per category and not once per mention, so a cell reading asthma, asthma is one record with asthma; the duplicate mentions are counted and reported separately, since a column full of them is usually a concatenation that ran twice rather than a fact. A record with no values at all is still a record and stays in the denominator, because removing it would raise every percentage in the table. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network.

capabilities.name: Which values appear together, with lift so a big pair is not mistaken for a real association
capabilities.notes: Pair frequency across several category columns, or within one multi-value column, with the number of records holding both. The arithmetic this refuses to hide is that a big pair count is usually just two common values meeting: if 60 percent of records have A and 60 percent have B, then roughly 36 percent will have both for no reason at all, and a table ranked by raw support ranks popularity while looking like it ranks association. So every pair ships count_a, count_b and a lift computed as visible division against what independence alone would predict, in the engine and in the generated SQL alike. Each unordered pair appears exactly once, enforced by an item_a < item_b inequality that also prevents a value pairing with itself; emitting the mirror image as well would double every count and inflate every share. Pairs resting on very few records are flagged as a hint rather than a measurement, because a lift of seven built on a single record is noise wearing a large number. In column mode each value is prefixed with its column name by default, since a value of yes in two different columns is not the same item and pairing them would be meaningless. Records with very many items are capped and any truncation is counted and stated rather than left to distort the totals. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network.

capabilities.name: Return within a window, as pairs plus two rates that admit where the data ran out
capabilities.notes: Index event to return event pairs plus a rate, for questions of the another one within thirty days shape. The load-bearing arithmetic is censoring: an event in the last N days of the data has not had N days to recur, so counting it as no return drags the rate down for calendar reasons that have nothing to do with the entities. Two rates are therefore reported side by side, one over the events that had a full window available and one over every event, alongside the number censored and the observation end being used; the panel stacks both above the pairs table so that on a tablet the answer is not the thing that scrolled off the right edge. An observation end can be given explicitly, for the common case where the export merely stopped rather than the world ending. Each index event pairs with only the NEXT event and never with every later one, so three events give two pairs rather than three and the count is not quadratically inflated by long-running entities. The smallest gap defaults to one day, which treats two events sharing a date as one event entered twice rather than as an instant return; a zero gap is available and the notes say what accepting it means. Events with a later next event beyond the window are counted separately, so widening the window is a visible decision rather than a discovery. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network.

capabilities.name: Standardise category values, where the proposal is not the map and nothing merges unconfirmed
capabilities.notes: Distinct values of a category column, proposed merge groups, a human-confirmed map, and a glass-box UPDATE. Nothing is applied without confirmation, and the proposal is deliberately not the map: proposeMergeGroups returns groups and no map at all, the panel lets any group be switched off before it counts, and validation refuses outright any configuration whose confirmed flag is not literally true. The default modes are deterministic (case, whitespace, punctuation) because those are reversible facts about the text rather than opinions about meaning; similarity scoring is a guess, so it only runs when a clusterer is handed in and every group it produces is labelled as a guess in its own reason field. Canonical choice prefers a tidy, deliberately capitalised spelling over the merely most frequent one, so a value with a stray leading space cannot win a tie and write that space into every row it absorbs. A chained recode, where a becomes b while b becomes c, is refused rather than resolved, because the resulting table depends on which replacement ran first and that is a coin flip and not a merge. An audit column captures the original value BEFORE the update, in that order in the generated SQL, since afterwards the old spelling exists nowhere and the merge could be neither reviewed nor undone. Columns that are nearly all distinct are called out as identifiers whose merging breaks joins, and sensitive categories are told that a merge there needs a stated reason rather than a similarity score. Pure ES module, Node-testable, no DuckDB and no network.

capabilities.name: Several numbers on one surface, each with the query that produced it in the same tile
capabilities.notes: A dashboard shows numbers and nowhere to look for how they were computed, so the argument in the meeting becomes about whether the person who made it is trustworthy. Every tile here carries the query underneath it, in the same tile, and the proof block is the shared GlassBox model rather than a second implementation, so proof reads the same here as it does under a SQL result. Every tile is arithmetic over the rows actually in memory, computed in JavaScript because DataGlow does not require a query engine to be present, with the equivalent SQL printed beside it so a person can take it to their own warehouse; test/proof-board.test.mjs pins the two against each other. Nothing is seeded: tilesFromDataset returns an empty list when there are no rows and the panel shows its empty state with one call to action. There is no default value, no zero fallback and no placeholder number anywhere, because showing 0 for a number nobody computed is inventing a KPI, and hasValue rejects NaN and blank strings so formatTileValue returns empty rather than a plausible-looking zero. A malformed tile is kept and marked incomplete with its reasons listed rather than dropped, since a board that looks complete and is quietly missing a number is much harder to notice.

capabilities.name: Not checked is a first-class badge that nothing can promote to passed
capabilities.notes: The tempting design is a green tick or nothing, which quietly turns no check has run into this passed. That is the single most expensive lie a surface like this can tell, so unknown is a badge with its own wording and its own sentence saying it is an absence of evidence rather than a pass. The badge is read off a real gate result when one is supplied; a caller that labels a tile clear while handing over a blocked verdict gets the gate result shown and the disagreement recorded as a problem on the tile. Nothing forges a gate either: the tile badge is deliberately not passed to GlassBox as a Publish-Safe verdict, because that would render a chip no gate ever produced, so a tile with no gate result shows GlassBox reporting the absence. Verify board checks the five things the board can actually check, that every tile carries its code, that every value was computed, that ids are unique, that a gate reported, and that all tiles describe one dataset, and it names the two it cannot: whether each query still returns the number shown, which would need the dataset and the engine and would report a fresh number as if it were the recorded one, and whether these are the right numbers to look at, which no check can answer.

capabilities.name: Glowbook: the board as one HTML file with no script, written only after a human says yes
capabilities.notes: A link to a result is a promise that a server will still be there showing the same thing, and DataGlow has no server, so a shared link would have to be a hosted copy of the data. A Glowbook is instead one self-contained file on the person's own disk: no script, no stylesheet link, no iframe, no fetch, nothing that loads. It is a document, not an application, because an exported page that runs code can differ from what the sender previewed and is also the thing a mail gateway quarantines. Every tile is written finding first and then the proof, the same order as the panel on screen, so a reader who has seen one does not have to relearn the other, and every value and query is escaped into the markup as text. The file will be forwarded to people who did not run the analysis and a page of green ticks reads as an audit, so the disclaimer is emitted from a constant a caller cannot edit away: it states that this is a record of how numbers were computed on one device, that a tile marked not checked has not passed anything, and that it is not a certification, not an audit, not a compliance claim and not legal or clinical advice. A separate line says the proof is readable code and not a cryptographic proof, so nobody reads it as zero-knowledge. The engine returns a string and never writes it; the canvas surface asks the person first, because only a surface can ask.

capabilities.name: Five coach steps that point at real controls, dismissed once and gone for good
capabilities.notes: A tour is usually a framework: an overlay, a backdrop, a step machine and a scroll lock, all of it built to hold attention, which is the wrong goal for someone who opened a panel because they had a job to do. These steps are a list of objects with a target element id. The strip points at the thing and says one sentence, nothing is dimmed, nothing is blocked, and the panel stays fully usable with it open. There is no video, because a video means an asset, an asset means a CDN and a CDN means the page reaches the network, which is the one claim this product cannot give up; text beside the control it describes also survives being read at 360px, which a 16:9 clip does not. A step whose target is missing is skipped rather than pointed at empty space, and an id lookup that throws drops the step rather than the strip. Once dismissed it stays dismissed, because a tip that returns on every open becomes an obstacle for exactly the person who has opened the panel most often, and unreadable storage is treated as never seen so a refused localStorage costs a tip and not the panel. Kept separate from the whole-app journey in analyst-journey.js, whose four moments are hard-coded to the landing, the drop, the pulse read and the finish and which publishes no way to register more, so it is shaped the same way rather than widened to carry a second concern.

capabilities.name: Stamping a tile composes the Trust Ledger rather than inventing a second chain
capabilities.notes: tileReceiptClaim assembles only the claim: the label, the value as it was formatted, a plain statement of what is being asserted, the query chain behind it, the validation state at the moment it was computed and the dataset fingerprint. It computes no hash and no commitment, because the hash chain already exists on the Trust Ledger and a second one written here would be a competing record of the same session. The canvas surface asks the person before appending the row and says in the prompt that the row stays on this device and is a record of what was computed rather than a certification. Portable receipts and the Proof Room are not present in this build, so the controls that would compose them are feature-detected and simply absent rather than mounted and failing: a link to a surface that does not exist is a dead end wearing a working button.

capabilities.name: Every number in a generated claim is bound to a tile or refused by name
capabilities.notes: A language model writing prose about a dataset will produce a number that reads correctly and was never computed, and the reader cannot tell the difference by looking. This gate does not ask the model to be careful. It extracts every number from the finished text and requires each one to match a Proof Board tile or an engine result, and it names the ones that do not instead of softening the claim around them. The tolerance is deliberate and narrow: an exact match, or a correct rounding to the precision the author actually wrote, and nothing else, so a claim cannot round 41.6 to about 45 and call it a summary. A tile carrying the blocked badge refuses outright, because a number a check has already objected to is the worst thing to quote; a tile carrying the unknown badge binds but raises a caution, because no check having run is not the same as a check having passed. ISO dates, clock times and dotted version strings are masked out before extraction, so the gate does not refuse the method line that ships with its own output. There is no override: the caller gets the refusal and the list of unbound numbers, and can delete them or go compute them.

capabilities.name: A proved number becomes a post draft without being retyped, and copy is the last thing the app does
capabilities.notes: The loop is analyze locally, prove on the Proof Board, publish, then post, and the last step is where analysts normally lose the proof: a number that survived a query engine, a validation gate and a receipt chain gets retyped by hand into a social post and becomes a number with nothing behind it. So the draft here is not written and then checked. It is assembled from tiles, which means every number in it came out of an engine by construction, and then it is checked anyway through the prove gate, because assembly can still go wrong and a post is not something you can recall. NEVER_AUTO_POST is a constant rather than a setting: DataGlow has no server and no outbound network so an OAuth posting integration would need both, and beyond that a tool that can post on your behalf is a tool that can post something you did not read. The output is text on a clipboard and the last action is always a human pasting it. The transparency line is computed from the badges actually present rather than written as a fixed string, because Numbers engine-checked is a claim about the work and it is false if any tile in the post is carrying the not checked badge, which is exactly the case where the reader most needs to know. A tile with no value is not a weaker bullet, it is not a bullet at all, and a blocked tile is excluded with its reason shown so the user can see why a number visible on the board is missing from the draft. Copy draft needs both a passing gate and a ticked review box.

capabilities.name: A Power BI or Tableau user gets the data, the dictionary, the queries and an honest validation summary
capabilities.notes: Handing a CSV to a BI team loses everything that made the analysis defensible: the column meanings, the queries, and what was and was not checked. This produces five plain files instead, data.csv, dictionary.md, queries.sql, validation-summary.md and README-handoff.md, and there is no zip because adding a compression dependency to turn five readable files into one opaque archive makes the output harder to inspect for no gain the recipient can feel. The CSV neutralises a leading equals, plus, minus or at sign so a cell cannot execute as a formula when the file is opened in a spreadsheet, which is the one way a pure text export can still hurt someone. The validation summary refuses to grade what it did not see: a null rate over zero rows is reported as not known rather than as zero percent, and a number with no recorded query is said to have none rather than being given a plausible-looking one. The README says in the first paragraph that this is not a certified deliverable, does not reproduce a dashboard, and is not endorsed by or certified with either tool, because the file most likely to be forwarded is the one most likely to be read as a claim. The download asks first.

capabilities.name: A readable receipt for the Safe Harbor screen that refuses to read as a clearance
capabilities.notes: The HIPAA Safe Harbor verifier already existed and already decided; this adds only the record of what it looked at and what it found, in markdown or as one self-contained HTML file, and computes no privacy verdict of its own so there is exactly one thing in the codebase that can say whether a column looks identifying. The renaming on the way out is the point: the engine verdict pass is printed as Nothing was flagged by this screen and never as the bare word it uses internally, because a receipt is precisely the artefact someone forwards to a stakeholder as evidence, and a document with a bare pass at the top will be read as a clearance no matter what the paragraph below it says. The non-certification disclaimer is emitted from a constant that a caller cannot remove or override, and the receipt states plainly what the screen cannot see: it reads column names and sampled values, so free text holding a name in the middle of a sentence, or a combination of columns that identifies someone only together, is outside what it can find. The exported HTML has no script, no stylesheet link, no iframe and no network reference, so the file is the same offline as online. The download asks first.

capabilities.name: A number read off a generated query can be kept as a tile that carries the query with it
capabilities.notes: The NL to SQL surface already showed the generated SQL before running it, which is the glass-box half of the promise. This is the other half: the number a person reads off the result can be kept on the Proof Board with the query that produced it attached, so it can later be quoted with something behind it rather than retyped from memory. The value is typed by the person who read the result and is never guessed: an empty box adds nothing rather than adding a zero, and the confirm says outright that no check has run on the number so the tile will carry the not checked badge until one does. Tiles added this way survive a board rebuild, because the board is rebuilt every time the panel opens and losing them silently would be worse than not offering the button.

capabilities.name: A persistent chip says whether the built-in model is running on this machine, and why it is not when it is not
capabilities.notes: DataGlow had been running a language model on the user own machine for months with nothing on the page that said so, which made the most distinctive property of the product invisible. The chip is always present and its state is derived on every render from four observed facts rather than stored: WebGPU presence, whether the model is loaded, whether Air-Gap Mode is on, and whether the model is already cached. A stored boolean would drift from the truth the moment any of those changed. The precedence is deliberate. Air-Gap outranks capability, because a session whose whole posture is that nothing goes out must not be told it could download a model. Capability outranks loadedness, because a loaded flag on a machine with no WebGPU is a stale flag and trusting it would put a ready chip on a page that cannot generate a word. A model already loaded does outrank Air-Gap, because running it sends nothing and Air-Gap only ever objects to the download. Every state carries the reason it is in that state, because a chip that says not available without saying why sends a person to a support page that does not exist.

capabilities.name: The local model registry names the alternatives that were considered and what is actually in the way of each
capabilities.notes: A registry with one entry is a constant wearing a costume. This one lists five options with what is true about each: download size, licence, runtime, and what happens on web, desktop and mobile. Exactly one is marked shipped and the rest carry an honest fit value, so nobody reads the list as a menu of things they can switch to today. The Llama entry names its licence as a community licence that is not OSI approved rather than glossing it, which is the reason it is not the default in a tool people ship work from. The shipped identifier is not retyped here on trust: a test reads MODEL_ID and MODEL_LABEL out of js/narrative/ondevice-llm.js and fails if the registry and the loader ever disagree.

capabilities.name: A model rephrase that introduces a number the engine did not produce is discarded, not shown
capabilities.notes: The Guarded Copilot Tier 2 prompt already asked the model not to invent numbers. That is the correct thing to put in a prompt and it is not a control. A model that transposes 1204 into 1240, or rounds 47.3 percent to nearly half and then writes 50 percent, has done exactly what language models do, and the result is a wrong number in a confident sentence with no mark on it. This makes the request a control. The Tier 1 deterministic text is ground truth, its numbers become the permitted set, and the Bundle 10 prove gate does the comparing including its rounding policy: a number rendered to fewer places still binds, a different number does not. A failing rephrase falls back to the deterministic text verbatim rather than having its numbers stripped, because a sentence with the numbers taken out is worse than the plain sentence it was meant to improve and nobody can tell by looking that it was edited. When no guard is reachable at all the copilot also falls back, because an unchecked rephrase is not a passing one. The guard lives outside guarded-copilot.js so that module keeps its frozen four function read-only surface.

capabilities.name: A continuous strip reports the state of the proof and answers no question about the data
capabilities.notes: Operating system level ambient assistants are always watching and always willing to answer, and that combination is the failure mode: the thing is never allowed to say it does not know, so it says something. DataGlow answer is the opposite half. The strip is continuous but it reports rather than generates: last prove gate result, Air-Gap state, open caveat count, and drift severity when a watchdog reported one. Two refusals are load bearing. First, answerAmbientQuestion exists and always declines with a reason and a redirect to a surface where the answer comes from a query you can read, so adding an answer path later is a deliberate act rather than a convenience. Second, a prove result that ran against an earlier version of the data is reported as stale rather than as a pass, because a green tick for yesterday data is worse than no strip at all. Nothing checked yet is reported as an absence and never as a pass, and Air-Gap being off is not spun as a positive.

capabilities.name: What this machine can do, with a does-not line for every does line
capabilities.notes: Every tool that runs SQL says it runs SQL and every one of them means a different SQL. The gap between what a person hears and what the software does is where trust goes, and it goes quietly. Seven areas are written down with a does line and a separate does-not line that cannot be skimmed past: SQL is real DuckDB in a tab and is not every warehouse dialect, Python is real CPython through Pyodide and truncates the bridge at a stated row limit, R is WebR and is not CRAN, Excel Hell Repair repairs the data in a workbook and does not read VBA or formulas, size is comfortable through the low millions of rows and is not any size, a messy file is solved here while a messy data estate is not, and local execution is a privacy property and not a compliance one. The row limit is a parameter with a documented default rather than a second copy of the number, because a copy would go stale the first time someone tuned the real one and this module would then be confidently telling users a limit the product no longer has. A test reads PY_BRIDGE_ROW_LIMIT out of js/runtimes-viz/python-runtime.js and pins the default to it. The ceiling can be copied out as markdown, behind the same human confirm as every other outbound path.

capabilities.name: The Polars path reports whether Polars is reachable and never claims it is ready
capabilities.notes: Polars keeps being the right answer to a question DataGlow does not have. It is genuinely fast, people ask for it by name, and a chip saying Polars ready would be the cheapest way to look more serious than the product is. So this ships as a status and contains no engine. Three states only: available when the Pyodide session can actually import it, not installed when it cannot, and not applicable when no Python session is running. There is no fourth state meaning coming soon, because a state nobody can currently be in is a promise wearing the costume of a status. No input and garbage input both refuse to yield available, so the chip cannot fake ready. DuckDB remains the analytical engine and every availability object restates that, because the risk with a second dataframe path is not that it is slow, it is that someone assumes their query silently went somewhere they did not pick.

capabilities.name: Every runtime this build downloads is pinned to an exact version at a named origin, and the CSP is derived from that list
capabilities.notes: The privacy claim is about egress and it is true, but four heavy runtimes are still fetched from public CDNs and each one is code that will run over the file someone just opened. Subresource Integrity does not reach either of them: WebLLM arrives through a dynamic import, which takes no integrity attribute, and the weights are over a gigabyte fetched in shards by the runtime itself. So the control is a pinned immutable version URL plus a short allowlist of origins, written once here instead of spelled slightly differently in four loaders. One runtime resolves through a floating path and is recorded with pinned false and reported as a finding, because a supply-chain module that lists only what is already fine is decoration. Model ids are an allowlist rather than a text box, since a model id is a path into a remote registry and accepting one from user input is accepting an arbitrary download instruction. The CSP is computed from the same pin list rather than typed, which is how it caught a real shipping bug: the desktop shell permitted two CDNs no loader uses while blocking the three the product depends on, so WebLLM, WebR and the weights were silently dead on desktop. Three residuals are named with what each costs: unsafe-inline, unsafe-eval and the CDN origins themselves.

capabilities.name: The built-in AI chip can reach ready, because loaded now means an engine exists rather than a download having started
capabilities.notes: The status chip shipped with nothing to read. The inlined window.OnDeviceLLM footer published four names the module has never exported, so all four resolved to a null, a function returning false, a null and an empty array, and the chip could not distinguish a loaded model from an absent one. Worse, isModelLoaded returned enginePromise != null, which is true from the instant someone clicks through the entire multi-minute weight download, so a chip built on it would have said ready while nothing could run. Loaded and loading are now separate observed facts, both cleared when a load fails and both cleared by clearModelCache. The four legacy names stay published because something may read them and a sudden undefined is worse than a null.

capabilities.name: A start-here rail showing Drop, Ask, Prove, Ship and Compound, read from what is on screen rather than from a stored step counter
capabilities.notes: The product has the pieces of a coherent path and no visible path. The rail is five steps and it deletes nothing: every tab, panel and button stays exactly where it was, because removing surfaces is a redesign and this is a signpost. Each step is marked done, current, todo or skipped from observed state rather than from a stored counter, so refreshing the page or arriving mid-session does not reset a progress bar that was never measuring progress. Shipping without proving is reported as skipped rather than quietly counted as done, because that is the one sequence worth naming. A step whose target surface is not mounted in this build renders as text and says so, since a button that opens nothing is worse than a sentence. Dismissing the rail is remembered and leaves a small chip to bring it back.

capabilities.name: The desktop llama.cpp sidecar path is complete and honest about the binary not being in this build
capabilities.notes: A desktop build can run a much larger model than a browser tab, through a llama.cpp server shipped beside the app as a Tauri sidecar. The binary is not in this build and pretending otherwise is the failure this module exists to prevent, so the states are exact: unavailable_web in a browser, sidecar_missing on a desktop build with no binary, ready only when one is actually present, and error when the sidecar is there and failed. Running in a browser outranks everything, because a browser cannot have a sidecar under any circumstances and a status that reports otherwise is broken rather than optimistic. bundledInThisBuild is a constant false rather than a computed value, since the honest answer today does not depend on anything observable at runtime. tauri.bundle.externalBin stays an empty array on purpose: Tauri resolves each entry to a per-target-triple file at bundle time, so a named entry with no binary behind it fails the desktop build rather than shipping a promise. describeSidecarScaffold writes down the five steps and the exact config path, so turning this on later is an edit rather than an investigation.

capabilities.name: SQL starter material that leads with what DuckDB will not do and then hands over ten queries that run
capabilities.notes: Ten snippets for the queries people rewrite from scratch every time: latest row per key, duplicate keys, a null audit, an anti-join, join fan-out, a month spine, a running total, an unpivot, top N per group and a table profile. Each one names the placeholders to replace, because a query run against a table called your_table is a wasted click. Twelve places DuckDB and Postgres part company are listed with both dialects side by side and which of the two is the odd one out, since the expensive way to learn that QUALIFY exists in one and not the other is at three in the morning against a warehouse. Copy is the only action: the panel never runs anything and never writes into an editor behind your back.

capabilities.name: Python starter cells that state the bridge row limit before the first recipe rather than after a wrong answer
capabilities.notes: Pyodide is real CPython with real pandas, and the thing that catches people is not a missing library, it is that the dataframe crossing the bridge is capped. A truncated frame gives an answer that is the right shape and the wrong number, and nothing on screen says so. The truncation notice is therefore the first thing in the tab and it states the delivered row count against the real one. The default limit is a documented parameter and a test reads PY_BRIDGE_ROW_LIMIT out of js/runtimes-viz/python-runtime.js and pins the default to it, so the fallback and the truth cannot drift apart silently. What is not there is listed plainly: no pip install from the network, no local file access, no database driver. Polars is reported as unavailable rather than unknown, because nothing in this build imports it.

capabilities.name: R starter cells that list what cannot run in this session with the reason, rather than hiding it
capabilities.notes: WebR is R and it is not CRAN. Two optional packages, jsonlite and ggplot2, may or may not have installed in a given session, and the kernel is the only thing that knows because it is what tried, so the canvas kernel now answers a packages() call instead of leaving anything outside to guess. Recipes needing a package that did not install are still listed, under a heading saying they cannot run here and naming which package is missing, because a person who came looking for ggplot needs to learn that in the panel rather than from an error. Absent any answer the pack assumes neither installed, which marks more recipes unavailable than may be true; overstating what installed is the worse error, since it hands out a call that fails. Base R plotting is always available and is offered as the fallback rather than presented as a consolation.

capabilities.name: SUMMARIZE promoted to Proof Board tiles, CSV rejects surfaced, and eleven more SQL recipes
capabilities.notes: Running SUMMARIZE against the active table turns null rates and distinctness into Proof Board tiles marked unknown until a person reviews them, never auto-graded. Eleven more recipes cover pivot and unpivot, group by all, select exclude and replace, moving windows, share of total and a profile query, each still copy-only. The CSV load path now runs with ignore_errors and store_rejects so a malformed line lands in a quarantine panel instead of silently vanishing, with the option to keep the good rows or abandon the load.

capabilities.name: A CSV load quarantine that reads DuckDB's rejected rows before dropping them, with a keep-good-rows or abandon-load choice and a receipt either way
capabilities.notes: DuckDB's ignore_errors/store_rejects already computed a rejects table on CSV load; it was being read only for a count and then dropped. buildQuarantine() reads the actual reject rows and reasons before the temporary tables are dropped, and offers exactly two choices, keep the rows that parsed or abandon the load, never a silent default. quarantineReceiptLine() writes a record on either outcome. Surfaced from the SQL power pack drawer behind the sqlPowerDeepen flag.

capabilities.name: Import-time scan for values at risk of silent type coercion, such as a gene symbol read as a date
capabilities.notes: Six rules catch both already-coerced values, a date that used to be a gene symbol, scientific notation that used to be an ID, and values still at risk in this column. The only action offered is holding the column as text; the person reviewing decides, and every outcome (clean, applied, overridden) is written to the receipt line.

capabilities.name: A real polars, scikit-learn, statsmodels and pyarrow probe, with recipes gated on what it finds
capabilities.notes: The Bundle 11 polars status was a hard-coded false. The probe cell here uses importlib.util.find_spec against all four packages and reports unknown, available or not_loaded; nine recipes for polars, scikit-learn and statsmodels are only shown live once the probe says so, with the rest listed as not runnable and why.

capabilities.name: dplyr, tidyr and base R recipes gated on real package state, with Air-Gap Mode blocking any install
capabilities.notes: The WebR startup path previously called installPackages with no Air-Gap or offline check, so Air-Gap Mode did not stop the fetch. rPackageInstallAllowed() now gates that call and reports which of the two blocked it; ten more recipes (dplyr verbs, base aggregate and crosstab, ggplot skeletons) are listed as not runnable with the specific reason, air gap, offline, or simply not installed, rather than hidden.

capabilities.name: Ready, partial or missing status for the DuckDB-to-Python bridge, with the 200,000-row JSON ceiling stated
capabilities.notes: The bridge today is JSON rows, capped at 200,000, never described as unlimited. The status chip reports ready, partial or missing from whether pyarrow is actually probed present, and the four concrete steps left before an Arrow-native path exists are listed with which are done today (only the pyarrow probe) and which are not (exposing an Arrow result, writing a shared buffer, raising the limit).

capabilities.name: A plain statement that Power Query M is not embedded, with the concrete DataGlow equivalent for each M step
capabilities.notes: Five common Power Query M steps are matched to their DataGlow equivalent across Excel Hell, DuckDB SQL, Python and R, and the note states plainly that for M-only enterprise workbooks the hand-off is still export. The same note is folded into the capability ceiling as its own group, not buried inside Excel.

capabilities.name: A packaging path and status for the desktop llama.cpp sidecar binary, present only when the binary is present
capabilities.notes: scripts/fetch-llama-sidecar.mjs places a per-target-triple binary into src-tauri/binaries/, which is git-ignored and never committed: tens of megabytes per triple with no model weights ever included. The script does not run in CI and does not touch tauri.conf.json. checkPackagingAgreement() catches the case where Tauri's externalBin config and the actual on-disk binary disagree, so a build never silently claims a sidecar that is not there.

capabilities.name: An append-only Repair Ledger of every step this session, the Applied Steps list Power Query has and DataGlow did not
capabilities.notes: A plain, in-memory, append-only array of steps, each with an id, timestamp, kind, engine (sql/python/r/excel/system), the code or recipe id, input/output table hint, a receipt-friendly summary, and a status of applied, skipped, failed, or proposed. Export as JSON or Markdown; a step that is a pure SQL insert can offer a re-run plan that hands back the exact code and never executes it. The panel opens from the power packs SQL tab (PQ-parity section) rather than a new top-nav item. Best-effort wiring appends from the Excel type guard, SUMMARIZE profiling, and PQ-parity/SQL recipe copies; CSV quarantine and Excel Hell apply are not yet wired and wiringReport() names the gap rather than hiding it.

capabilities.name: Fifteen DuckDB SQL templates matching the Power Query step shapes, never M
capabilities.notes: Promote headers, change type, fill down/up, split column, merge (left/inner/full), append (UNION BY NAME), group by, unpivot (dynamic EXCLUDE form), pivot, remove duplicates, replace/trim/clean, and a fuzzy-join sketch using jaro_winkler_similarity with an explicit O(n*m) warning. Each card names the DuckDB SQL, why it matters, and the placeholders to replace. Power Query M is not embedded and is not the substitute claimed; the Repair Ledger is named as the Applied Steps equivalent. Reuses powerQueryHonestNote's stance rather than repeating it.

capabilities.name: Four-state Arrow bridge transfer status (arrow_ipc/batch_bridge/json_bridge/missing) plus a working typed-array batch path
capabilities.notes: DuckDB-WASM in this page still does not expose an Arrow result buffer, so arrow_ipc is not reachable yet; that ceiling is stated, not hidden. batch_bridge is real: values are encoded into a typed array plus a null mask, decoded back, and proven correct on a small fixed fixture with roundTripFixture(), which is a correctness check and not a timing benchmark. The row ceiling is unchanged (JSON_BRIDGE_ROW_LIMIT) until there is actual evidence for a higher one; BATCH_BRIDGE_CEILING says so explicitly. Superset of the Bundle 13 ready/partial/missing status, which is unchanged for any caller still using buildArrowBridgeStatus().

capabilities.name: Dry-run and three-state fetch status (missing/fetched_unwired/ready) for the desktop llama.cpp sidecar binary
capabilities.notes: node scripts/fetch-llama-sidecar.mjs --dry-run prints the exact destination and next command without creating a directory or writing a file. --status reports missing (nothing on disk), fetched_unwired (vendored but tauri.bundle.externalBin does not declare it, or checkPackagingAgreement() disagrees), or ready (vendored, declared, and the agreement holds) for the host target triple. This is a packaging claim, not a runtime handshake result; buildDesktopLlmStatus() in js/ai/desktop-local-llm.js is the only module that ever reports the sidecar as actually answering requests. Documented in docs/desktop-llama-sidecar.md. No binary of any kind is committed; src-tauri/binaries/ stays git-ignored.

capabilities.name: Four project-fit lane cards (SQL, Python, Excel, R) naming when to stay and when to hand off, never any project
capabilities.notes: SQL and Python are named as able to carry a whole project within stated limits (SQL: DuckDB dialect, no scheduled jobs; Python: bridge row ceiling, no native wheels or GPU). Excel and R are named as partial: Excel repairs and exports but is not a VBA or Power Pivot replacement, R covers tidy summary and plot recipes in webR but not full CRAN or heavy statistical modeling. Every card names a concrete hand-off target. Rendered as its own 'Project fit' tab in the power packs panel rather than folded into an existing tab, since it answers a different question than any single runtime's snippet list.
